title: Filing an Income-Tax Return
summary: GATHER → FILE → ASSESS → REPEAT NEXT YEAR
subtitle: Most people dread tax season before they’ve even opened a single form. For most Canadians, filing takes less time than a load of laundry.

blocks.text: Most people dread tax season before they’ve even opened a single form.
Here’s the truth. For most Canadians, filing a return takes less time than a load of laundry. Software does the math, and the CRA fills in many of the boxes for you.
What causes trouble isn’t the filing. It’s not knowing what to do, or waiting so long that a small task turns into a stressful one.
This lesson walks through the whole process, start to finish, in plain steps.
File on time every year and collect every benefit you’re owed.
blocks.detail: A return filed on time protects you from penalties and unlocks payments like the GST/HST credit and the Canada Child Benefit.
blocks.extra: Section 03 lays out this year’s dates in order.

sections.title: Do you even need to file?

blocks.text: Short answer: almost always yes, even with little or no income.
You must file if you owe tax, if the CRA asks you to, or if you’re self-employed. But here’s what most people miss: you should file even when none of those apply.

Filing is how you unlock benefits: the GST/HST credit, the Canada Child Benefit and provincial credits. None of these are paid on their own. They are worked out from your tax return. Skip filing, and you skip the benefit, even if you would have qualified for every dollar.
Zero income is not a reason to skip filing. It’s often the strongest reason to file.

items.title: “If I made no money this year, there’s no point filing.”
items.text: This is backwards. A year with little or no income is often the year you qualify for the most in benefits and credits. Filing with zero income costs you nothing and can put real money in your pocket.

blocks.text: A handful of dates matter each year. Here they are in order, for the 2025 return filed in 2026.

items.title: Late February. T4s and other tax slips arrive by mail or in your CRA account. NETFILE, the online filing system, opens around the same time.
April 30. The deadline for most Canadians to file, and to pay anything owed.
June 15. The filing deadline if you or your spouse are self-employed. But any money owed is still due April 30, even with the later filing date.

blocks.text: The gap between April 30 and June 15 trips people up every year. Filing late is one problem. Paying late is a separate, more costly one.
CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: SELF-EMPLOYED? TWO DEADLINES, NOT ONE

If you’re self-employed, you get extra time to file, until June 15. Many people hear that and relax. But the CRA still wants any money you owe by April 30, like everyone else. Miss that, and interest starts on May 1, no matter when you file. The fix is simple: file any time before June 15, but if you think you’ll owe, make a payment, even an estimate, by April 30. You can settle the difference later.

NETFILE, with software. The most common route. You use CRA-certified software, and several free options exist, to prepare your return and send it online. It’s fast, and your Notice of Assessment often arrives within two weeks.

Auto-fill my return. This is a feature inside NETFILE software, not a separate way to file. Sign in to your CRA account, and the software pulls in your T4s, T5s, RRSP contributions and more. Less typing, fewer mistakes.

A tax professional, using EFILE. An accountant or tax preparer files for you, for a fee. It’s worth it when your situation is complicated: self-employment, rental income, or a big life change like a divorce or an inheritance.

Free help exists too. Volunteer tax clinics (CVITP) prepare simple returns at no cost for people with a modest income. And if your income is low and simple, the CRA may invite you to use SimpleFile, which lets you file by answering a few short questions by phone or online.

items.title: “I need to hire an accountant every year or I’ll do it wrong.”
items.text: Most Canadians with simple job income can file correctly using free certified software in under an hour. Save the accountant for the years your situation gets complicated: self-employment, a big life change, or investment income you’re unsure how to report.

blocks.text: You’ll get a Notice of Assessment. Think of it as the CRA’s receipt. It confirms what they received, what they worked out, and whether you owe money or get a refund.
Filed online with direct deposit set up? Refunds can land in as little as eight business days. Paper returns take about eight weeks.

Keep that Notice of Assessment. It shows your RRSP room for next year, and it’s often the fastest way to prove your income if a lender or landlord asks. Spot a mistake later? You can ask the CRA to change a return from any of the past ten years.
CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: LATE FILING COSTS MORE THAN YOU’D THINK

Miss the deadline and owe money? The penalty starts at 5% of the balance owing, plus 1% for every full month you’re late, up to twelve months. Been late before? The CRA can double it for repeat cases: 10%, plus 2% a month for up to twenty months. Here’s the part people miss: the penalty is for filing late, not just paying late. Even if you can’t pay what you owe right now, file on time anyway, then ask the CRA for a payment arrangement. A late return costs far more than an on-time return with a payment plan.

items.title: I have all my tax slips: T4, T5, tuition receipts and anything else that applies to me.
I know whether I’m filing by April 30 or June 15.
If I’m self-employed, I know my payment is still due April 30, regardless of my filing deadline.
I’ve set up direct deposit with the CRA, for a faster refund if I’m owed one.
I’m filing even if I had little or no income this year.
I know where to find free help if my situation feels complicated.

blocks.text: Mateo’s first return
paragraphs: Mateo got his first job the summer he turned nineteen, loading trucks at a warehouse in Mississauga for minimum wage. When his T4 came the next February, he tossed it in a drawer. The amount was so small that filing a return didn’t seem worth the trouble.
He did the same thing the next two years. His part-time income was modest, and he figured the CRA had bigger fish to fry.
At twenty-two, Mateo applied for a student line of credit to finish his last year of college. The bank asked for his latest Notice of Assessment. He didn’t have one, for any year.

He had two choices. He could give up on the line of credit and take extra shifts, which would cost him study time in his final term. Or he could face three years of unfiled returns, which felt like opening a door he had kept shut. He booked a spot at his campus’s free tax clinic before he could change his mind.

A volunteer helped him file all three years in one afternoon. Then came the surprise. Because his income had been low, he had qualified for the GST/HST credit in each of those years. The CRA paid him more than $900 he had never claimed, money that had been waiting on a form nobody filled in.
Mateo got his Notice of Assessment and his line of credit. Now he files every year the same week his T4 arrives, and the drawer holds nothing but takeout menus.

blocks.text: File every year, even with little or no income. It’s how you unlock benefits like the GST/HST credit. Most Canadians file by April 30. Self-employed filers get until June 15, but any money owed is still due April 30. File on time even if you can’t pay in full, since the late-filing penalty costs more than a payment plan. And keep your Notice of Assessment. You’ll need it more often than you expect.
A twenty-minute habit each spring can pay you back for years.
blocks.detail: Filing on time keeps your benefits flowing and gives you the proof lenders and landlords ask for.

blocks.text: Worksheet: your filing plan

items.title: T4
items.text: The slip your employer issues showing your income and deductions for the year.

items.title: NETFILE
items.text: The CRA’s system for submitting your return electronically through certified software.

items.title: Auto-fill My Return
items.text: A feature that pulls your CRA-held slips directly into your tax software.

items.title: Notice of Assessment
items.text: The CRA’s summary after it processes your return, showing what you owe or get back.

items.title: Late-filing penalty
items.text: A charge of 5% of your balance owing, plus 1% per full month late, when you file after the deadline and owe money.

items.title: CVITP
items.text: Community Volunteer Income Tax Program. Free tax clinics for people with a modest income and a simple return.
